title: WHY DID ISH-BOSHETH CARE SO MUCH WHETHER ABNER HAD SLEPT WITH HIS FATHER’S CONCUBINE?
paragraphs: WHY DID ISH-BOSHETH CARE SO MUCH WHETHER ABNER HAD SLEPT WITH HIS FATHER’S CONCUBINE?

One accusation about a woman nearly destroyed a kingdom. But behind the bedroom scandal was a terrifying struggle for power, a wounded king, a furious general, and a warning about what happens when people try to hold on to what God is already taking away.
“And Saul had a concubine, whose name was Rizpah, the daughter of Aiah: and Ishbosheth said to Abner, Wherefore hast thou gone in unto my father's concubine?” — 2 Samuel 3:7 (KJV)
Imagine being a king and discovering that the most powerful man in your kingdom may have crossed a line so dangerous that it could cost you your throne.
Not by raising an army against you.
Not by publicly declaring himself king.
Not even by drawing a sword.
But by allegedly entering the bed of a woman who once belonged to your dead father's royal household.
And imagine knowing that the man you were about to confront was the very man who had helped put you on the throne.
You needed him.
You feared him.
And now you suspected that he might be preparing to replace you.
That is the world of 2 Samuel 3.
And if you read this passage as merely a dispute over sexual morality, you will miss one of its most disturbing revelations.
Because Ish-bosheth's question was not simply, "Did you sleep with her?"
Underneath it was another question.
"Are you trying to take my father's throne?"
And beneath that question was an even more painful one.
"Was I ever really king at all?"
This is where the story becomes painfully human.
Because sometimes the thing that makes us furious is not the thing that happened.
It is what we are afraid that thing means.
And sometimes our deepest insecurity is exposed by the very person we have trusted to keep us standing.
But before we enter that confrontation, we need to understand how a dead king's concubine became the center of a political crisis.
Saul was dead.
Israel's first king had fallen in battle. His sons Jonathan, Abinadab, and Malchi-shua had died with him (1 Samuel 31:2–6). The nation was fractured, and its future was uncertain.
David, whom God had chosen and Samuel had anointed years earlier, was ruling over Judah from Hebron.
But the rest of Israel had not yet united under David.
Abner, Saul's military commander, had taken Ish-bosheth, another son of Saul, and established him as king over Israel (2 Samuel 2:8–10).
Think about that.
Ish-bosheth wore the crown, but Abner commanded the military power that helped sustain his reign.
The king had a title.
Abner had influence.
The king occupied the throne.
Abner had helped place him there.
And Scripture gives us an extraordinary detail that explains why their relationship was so dangerous.
"Now Abner had made himself strong for the house of Saul." — 2 Samuel 3:6 (KJV)
The Hebrew says:
וְאַבְנֵר הָיָה מִתְחַזֵּק בְּבֵית שָׁאוּל
Ve-Avner hayah mitchazzeq be-veit Sha'ul.
The key word is מִתְחַזֵּק (mitchazzeq), from the Hebrew root חזק (ḥ-z-q), associated with strength, firmness, and becoming strong.
The wording portrays Abner as strengthening himself or consolidating his position within Saul's house.
This matters enormously.
Abner was not an insignificant servant accused of an indiscretion.
He was a powerful military leader whose influence was increasing during a civil war.
And Ish-bosheth was the king whose authority depended heavily upon him.
Then came Rizpah.
Scripture identifies her as Saul's concubine, the daughter of Aiah.
Her Hebrew name is רִצְפָּה (Ritzpah).

She was not simply an unnamed woman introduced to make a political story more dramatic. She was a real person whose life was entangled with the royal household, and whose later suffering would be recorded in one of the Bible's most heartbreaking scenes.
But here, in 2 Samuel 3, she is at the center of an accusation.
Ish-bosheth confronted Abner:
מַדּוּעַ בָּאתָה אֶל־פִּילֶגֶשׁ אָבִי
Maddua bata el-pilegesh avi?
Literally, the question is:
"Why have you gone in to my father's concubine?"
The expression "gone in to" is a biblical Hebrew idiom that can refer to sexual intercourse.
The word פִּילֶגֶשׁ (pilegesh) means "concubine," a woman recognized within a household in a relationship of lower status than that of a principal wife.

We should not romanticize that institution. Ancient royal households often operated within structures of unequal power, and Scripture's description of such arrangements does not mean God endorses every aspect of them.
But why would Ish-bosheth care so much?
Because in the ancient royal world, access to the former king's women could carry implications of succession, authority, and a claim upon royal privilege.
It was not merely about intimacy.
It could be interpreted as a political statement.
And the Bible itself gives us compelling reasons to understand why.
Remember what happened when David's son Absalom rebelled against him?
Absalom did not merely seize Jerusalem.
Following Ahithophel's counsel, he publicly entered into sexual relations with his father's concubines.
"So they spread Absalom a tent upon the top of the house; and Absalom went in unto his father's concubines in the sight of all Israel." — 2 Samuel 16:22 (KJV)
Why would Absalom do something so publicly disgraceful?
Because it was intended to make his rebellion unmistakable and deepen the division between himself and David.
It was a shocking assertion that he had displaced his father.
The women were treated as instruments of political humiliation.
And the terrible consequences of that act did not disappear when the rebellion ended.
Now consider another moment.
After David's death, Adonijah asked to marry Abishag the Shunammite, the young woman who had attended David in his old age.
Solomon reacted with extraordinary severity.
"And king Solomon answered and said unto his mother, And why dost thou ask Abishag the Shunammite for Adonijah? ask for him the kingdom also." — 1 Kings 2:22 (KJV)
Notice Solomon's reasoning.
He interpreted the marriage request as having implications for the throne.

The circumstances were not identical. Scripture explicitly says David had not been sexually intimate with Abishag (1 Kings 1:4), and the narrative does not identify her as a concubine in the same way it identifies Rizpah.
Nevertheless, the parallel is illuminating.
In Israel's royal narratives, a relationship with a woman associated with the former king could become a matter of political legitimacy.
That is the world in which Ish-bosheth confronted Abner.
And suddenly, his anger becomes understandable.
If Abner had taken Saul's concubine, Ish-bosheth could have viewed it as a declaration that Abner considered himself entitled to royal privileges.
Perhaps even to the throne.
But here is something we must not overlook.
The Bible never explicitly tells us whether Abner actually slept with Rizpah.
It records Ish-bosheth's accusation.
It records Abner's furious response.
But it does not independently confirm the alleged act.
We must not turn an accusation into a proven fact simply because it makes the story more dramatic.
And that distinction matters.
Especially for anyone who has ever been condemned by a rumor.
Anyone who has watched suspicion become certainty in someone else's mind.
Anyone who has suffered because another person decided that an accusation was enough.
Abner's response was explosive.

"Then was Abner very wroth for the words of Ishbosheth, and said, Am I a dog's head, which against Judah do shew kindness this day unto the house of Saul thy father, to his brethren, and to his friends, and have not delivered thee into the hand of David, that thou chargest me to day with a fault concerning this woman?" — 2 Samuel 3:8 (KJV)
Can you hear the indignation?
Abner was essentially protesting that after everything he had done for Saul's family, Ish-bosheth was accusing him of wrongdoing concerning a woman.
His words reveal the resentment beneath the surface.
He had defended Saul's house.
He had supported Ish-bosheth.
He had refused to hand him over to David.
And now the king was questioning him.
But what happened next was astonishing.
Abner declared that he would transfer the kingdom to David.
"So do God to Abner, and more also, except, as the LORD hath sworn to David, even so I do to him." — 2 Samuel 3:9 (KJV)
Read that again.
Abner acknowledged that the LORD had sworn concerning David's kingship.
This is one of the most revealing moments in the entire chapter.
The man who had been fighting to sustain Saul's dynasty now spoke as someone who knew that David's rise was consistent with God's declared purpose.
That raises an uncomfortable question.
If Abner knew God's intention concerning David, why had he continued strengthening the rival kingdom?
Scripture does not disclose every motive within his heart.
We cannot confidently say whether pride, loyalty, ambition, political calculation, or some mixture of these drove his decisions.
But the tension is undeniable.
Abner had been supporting a political arrangement that stood against the kingdom God was establishing through David.
And when Ish-bosheth challenged him, he abruptly announced his intention to change sides.
Was that repentance?
Was it wounded pride?
Was it revenge?
Was it political self-preservation?
The text does not settle the question.
And that uncertainty is part of what makes the story so unsettling.
Because a person can speak correctly about God's will while still having deeply mixed motives.
A person can say the right spiritual words for the wrong personal reasons.
A person can change direction without necessarily surrendering the heart.
And before we judge Abner too quickly, we ought to ask ourselves something.
Have we ever done what was right only after doing what was wrong became personally uncomfortable?
Have we ever obeyed God only after our own plans collapsed?
Have we ever called something "God's will" when it also happened to serve our wounded pride?
That question is not meant to crush us.
It is meant to expose the places where we still need grace.
Because God is not interested merely in outward religious alignment.
He sees the heart.
And there is another person in this story who deserves our attention.
Ish-bosheth.
The king who started the confrontation.
The man who accused Abner.
The man who suddenly discovered that the general holding his kingdom together could abandon him.
Scripture says:
"And he could not answer Abner a word again, because he feared him." — 2 Samuel 3:11 (KJV)
There it is.
Fear.
Behind the royal title.
Behind the accusation.
Behind the confrontation.
Fear.
He could not even answer.
The man wearing the crown was afraid of the man serving beneath him.
What a devastating picture of authority without security.
A king who could question his general but could not withstand his anger.
A ruler whose position depended on someone he could not control.
A man who had a throne but did not have peace.
And this is where an ancient political confrontation begins to reach into modern lives.
Because you do not have to wear a crown to know what it feels like to depend on someone else's approval.
You do not have to command an army to know what it feels like when someone stronger than you threatens to walk away.
You do not have to live in a palace to understand the fear of losing the thing that gives you identity.
Some people are holding on to relationships because they are terrified of being alone.
Some are protecting positions because they cannot imagine who they would be without a title.
Some are pretending their marriages are healthy because admitting the truth feels unbearable.
Some are staying silent in the face of wrongdoing because the person responsible has too much influence over their lives.
Some are trying to maintain an image of strength while privately falling apart.
And some have built their entire sense of worth around something God never intended to become their foundation.
Maybe that is why this story feels so uncomfortable.
Because beneath the ancient politics is a question that still confronts us.
What happens when the thing you depend on for security is the very thing you are afraid to lose?
Ish-bosheth had inherited a royal name.
But he could not inherit Saul's strength.
He occupied a position Abner had helped secure.
But he could not command Abner's loyalty.
And when that loyalty began to collapse, his authority was exposed.
There is a difference between having a position and having a foundation.
A position can be taken.
A title can disappear.
Influential people can leave.
Public approval can turn overnight.
But the person whose deepest hope rests in the Lord has an anchor beyond these changing things.
That does not mean Christians will never experience betrayal, grief, instability, or fear.
It means those things do not have the final authority to define who we are in Christ.
And yet, we need to be careful here.
It would be easy to turn this story into a simple lesson about insecurity and miss the greater biblical tragedy.
This was not merely a conflict between two insecure men.
It was part of a divided kingdom marked by warfare, competing loyalties, ambition, and bloodshed.
The Lord had chosen David, but the path toward the united kingdom was filled with human sin.
Abner eventually negotiated with David.
David received him and sent him away in peace.
But Joab, David's commander, had another grievance.
Abner had killed Joab's brother Asahel during the earlier conflict, after warning Asahel to stop pursuing him (2 Samuel 2:18–23).
Joab later deceived Abner into returning and killed him (2 Samuel 3:26–27).
The general who had promised to help establish David's rule never lived to see that work completed.
And David did not celebrate Abner's murder.
He publicly mourned him, condemned the bloodshed, and declared his own innocence concerning the killing (2 Samuel 3:28–39).
Then the story grew darker.
When Ish-bosheth heard that Abner had died, his courage failed, and Israel was troubled (2 Samuel 4:1).
Two men eventually murdered Ish-bosheth in his own house while he was resting.
They brought his head to David, apparently expecting a reward.
Instead, David condemned their murder and ordered their execution (2 Samuel 4:5–12).
Think about the bitter irony.
A man who had feared losing his throne ultimately lost his life to men who thought killing him would gain them favor with the next king.
What began with a dispute over a concubine became part of a chain of betrayal, political collapse, and death.
But we must not pretend that the accusation against Abner alone caused everything that followed.
The kingdom was already divided.
The conflict was already underway.
And the ambitions and decisions of multiple people contributed to the tragedy.
Scripture gives us something deeper than a neat chain of cause and effect.
It shows us how destructive human power struggles can become when pride, fear, violence, and self-interest rule the heart.
And then there is Rizpah.
The woman whose name appeared at the center of the accusation.
Did anyone ask her what happened?
The passage records no answer from her.
No explanation.
No testimony.
No account of her feelings.
We are not told whether she consented to any alleged relationship, whether the accusation was true, or what she experienced during the confrontation.
Her silence in the narrative should not become an invitation for us to invent her story.
But it should make us notice something.
The men argued about power.
The woman was spoken about.
And years later, Scripture brings Rizpah before us again.
Not as a political accusation.
But as a grieving mother.
In 2 Samuel 21, two of her sons, Armoni and Mephibosheth, were among seven descendants of Saul handed over to the Gibeonites and put to death in connection with Saul's earlier violence against them.
Rizpah responded with an act of extraordinary mourning.

"And Rizpah the daughter of Aiah took sackcloth, and spread it for her upon the rock, from the beginning of harvest until water dropped upon them out of heaven, and suffered neither the birds of the air to rest on them by day, nor the beasts of the field by night." — 2 Samuel 21:10 (KJV)
Can you picture her?
A mother sitting beneath the open sky.
Guarding the bodies of her sons.
Driving away birds by day.
Driving away wild animals by night.
Remaining there through an extended season of grief.
The woman once mentioned in connection with a royal scandal now appears as a mother refusing to abandon her dead children.
And when David learned what she had done, he took action to gather and bury the remains of Saul, Jonathan, and those who had been executed (2 Samuel 21:11–14).
The Bible does not tell us everything Rizpah felt.
It does not give us the words she may have cried into the night.
But it gives us enough to recognize her humanity.
She was more than the concubine of a king.
More than the subject of an accusation.
More than a name in a political dispute.
She was a mother who suffered.
And her grief was not forgotten by the biblical narrator.
How many people have we reduced to a scandal without ever considering their suffering?
How many women have been discussed as though their only importance was their connection to powerful men?
How many families have been wounded by conflicts that began in pride and ended in grief?
How many people are carrying pain that never appears in the public version of their story?
This is why reading Scripture faithfully requires more than searching for dramatic secrets.
We must pay attention to what God has actually revealed.
We must refuse to turn speculation into doctrine.
We must recognize the people whose suffering appears between the lines.
And above all, we must allow the whole counsel of Scripture to lead us to Jesus Christ.
Because the story of Ish-bosheth and Abner is not, by itself, a direct prophecy of Jesus.
We should not force every character to symbolize Christ or invent hidden meanings the text does not establish.
But when we read this account within the unfolding biblical story, a powerful contrast emerges.
The kingdom of Saul was collapsing.
David's kingdom was being established.
Yet even David, God's anointed king, was not a sinless savior.
David himself would later commit grievous sins, abuse royal power, and bring terrible suffering upon others.
The Bible refuses to present Israel's earthly kings as humanity's ultimate hope.
The history of the monarchy points beyond itself.
Toward the need for a King whose righteousness would not fail.
A King whose authority would not depend on manipulation.
A King who would not need to seize another man's throne.
A King who would not exploit the vulnerable to establish His power.
A King who would conquer through obedience, sacrificial love, and victory over death.
Jesus Christ.
The promised Son of David.
The One whose kingdom has no end (Luke 1:32–33).
And look at the difference.
Earthly rulers feared losing their power.
Jesus, who possessed divine glory, humbled Himself.
Philippians 2:6–8 describes Christ's willing humiliation, culminating in His death on the cross.
He did not stop being divine.
He did not surrender His divine nature.
But He took the form of a servant and became obedient unto death.
The rulers in 2 Samuel struggled to secure their kingdoms.
Jesus willingly laid down His life to save sinners.
And He rose again.
"Wherefore God also hath highly exalted him, and given him a name which is above every name." — Philippians 2:9 (KJV)
Do you see the contrast?
Human ambition grasps.
Christ humbles Himself.
Human pride seeks control.
Christ obeys the Father.
Human sin leaves wounded people behind.
Christ offers forgiveness, reconciliation, and eternal life to those who come to Him in faith.
That is the Gospel.
Not merely that God can improve our circumstances.
Not merely that Jesus can help us feel better about our insecurities.
But that we have sinned against a holy God, that Jesus died for our sins, that He was buried, and that He rose again according to the Scriptures (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
And through Him, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
This is where the story stops being merely about Ish-bosheth's fear and begins to confront ours.
What are you still trying to protect that has become more important to you than obedience to God?
What truth have you refused to face because you fear what it might cost?
What relationship, reputation, possession, ministry position, or personal ambition has quietly become the place where you seek the security that only God can ultimately give?
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe you smile in church.
Maybe you post verses about trusting God.
Maybe you encourage everyone else to have faith.
But in private, you are exhausted.
You are afraid of being replaced.
Afraid of being forgotten.
Afraid of losing someone.
Afraid of losing everything you worked so hard to build.
And perhaps you have been trying to control people because you cannot control the future.
Perhaps you have been holding on so tightly that your hands have forgotten what surrender feels like.
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not asking you to pretend those fears are imaginary.
He is calling you to bring them into the light.
"Casting all your care upon him; for he careth for you." — 1 Peter 5:7 (KJV)
Not because every circumstance will immediately change.
Not because every person who betrayed you will return.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored in the way you hope.
But because His care is real even when your circumstances remain painful.
And there is something else.
Perhaps you are not identifying with Ish-bosheth.
Perhaps you see yourself in Abner.
You have defended something for years.
You have fought to keep a situation alive.
You have insisted you were right.
But somewhere deep inside, you know that your pride has been directing your decisions.
You know the apology you have refused to make.
You know the truth you have avoided.
You know the bitterness you keep rehearsing.
You know the person you have tried to punish because they wounded your ego.
And now you are standing at a crossroads.
You can continue defending your pride.
Or you can humble yourself before God.
The call of the Gospel is not to protect the appearance of righteousness.
It is to repent and trust the One who alone is righteous enough to save us.
"God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble." — James 4:6 (KJV)
Grace.
What a word.
Not permission to continue in sin.
Not a religious excuse for manipulation.
Not a promise that our actions will have no consequences.
Grace is God's undeserved favor toward sinners, revealed supremely through Jesus Christ.
Grace forgives.
Grace transforms.
Grace teaches us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
Grace brings us to the cross where our pride has nowhere left to hide.
And maybe the most difficult part of surrender is admitting that we cannot save ourselves.
Ish-bosheth could not secure his kingdom.
Abner could not control the outcome of his political decisions.
David could not establish a perfectly righteous earthly reign.
Rizpah could not undo the deaths of her sons.
And we cannot erase our own guilt by trying harder, looking stronger, or hiding better.
We need a Savior.
Not another image to maintain.
Not another title to defend.
Not another person to control.
A Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
If you are reading this with tears you cannot explain, do not mistake emotional conviction for hopelessness.
The call to repentance is also an invitation to mercy.
"Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out." — John 6:37 (KJV)
That is the promise of Christ.
You do not have to manufacture a perfect past before coming to Him.
You do not have to pretend your motives have always been pure.
You do not have to claim that you have never been afraid, jealous, proud, or broken.
Come honestly.
Confess your sin.
Turn to Christ.
Trust His finished work.
And ask Him to teach you to walk in obedience.
Because the deepest transformation is not that you finally gain control of everything around you.
It is that you belong to Jesus even when you cannot control what happens next.
And that changes the way you live.
You can tell the truth without making your reputation your god.
You can repent without believing your failures are your final identity.
You can seek reconciliation without demanding control over another person's response.
You can stand for righteousness without turning your wounded pride into a weapon.
You can grieve honestly without abandoning hope.
You can give generously without trying to purchase God's approval.
And you can serve Christ without needing everyone to know your name.
That is not weakness.
That is the freedom of belonging to a King who will never be overthrown.
And now I want to ask you something deeply personal.
What part of this story found you?
Was it Ish-bosheth's fear?
Abner's wounded pride?
Rizpah's silent suffering?
The danger of allowing power to corrupt relationships?
Or the realization that you have been seeking security in something that cannot save you?
Not to impress anyone.
Not to prove your spirituality.
But because sometimes an honest confession becomes the beginning of a conversation that helps another struggling believer realize they are not alone.
Your testimony does not replace Scripture.
But it can point someone back to the Savior revealed in Scripture.
Not merely to increase the reach of a post, but because someone among your family, friends, or followers may be quietly wrestling with the very questions this passage raises.
Or send this privately to someone who needs encouragement but may not be comfortable discussing their struggles publicly.
We want this community to be a place where people encounter Scripture, biblical truth, thoughtful discipleship, honest conviction, and the hope of Jesus Christ.
Because the goal is not simply to collect followers.
The goal is to help people become followers of Jesus.
There is something beautiful about believers voluntarily coming alongside a ministry to help make biblical teaching available to others.
Scripture encourages generosity toward faithful Gospel work.
Paul wrote:
"Even so hath the Lord ordained that they which preach the gospel should live of the gospel." — 1 Corinthians 9:14 (KJV)
And he also wrote:
"Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver." — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
Both truths matter.
Supporting Gospel ministry can be a meaningful act of Christian generosity.
But giving must never be presented as a way to buy God's favor, guarantee blessings, or prove that someone truly loves Jesus.
Your salvation is not for sale.
God's grace is not behind a paywall.
Think about the believer who cannot afford expensive study materials.
The new Christian who is desperate to understand the Bible.
The exhausted parent searching for a devotional that speaks to their struggle.
The young person questioning whether Jesus can truly forgive their past.
The person who opens Facebook late at night and encounters a Scripture-centered message that leads them to open their Bible again.
We cannot promise how God will use every article.
But we can faithfully keep pointing people to Christ.
We want biblical nourishment and opportunities for spiritual growth to remain accessible to people who need them.
It is not the heart of the invitation.
The heart is the opportunity to help sustain and expand a ministry dedicated to making Jesus known.
You can pray.
You can invite someone to read the Bible.
You can encourage another believer.
You can share a testimony of God's grace.
You can serve faithfully in your local church.
The kingdom of God is not measured by the amount of money a person can contribute.
What matters is faithfulness to Christ.
And that brings us back to the question that started this entire story.
Why did Ish-bosheth care so much whether Abner had slept with his father's concubine?
Because in the world of Israel's monarchy, such an act could signal a claim to royal authority.
Because Abner was already growing powerful.
Because Ish-bosheth's position was fragile.
Because the king feared the very general who had helped establish his rule.
And because an accusation involving Saul's concubine threatened to expose the instability of an already divided kingdom.
But the deeper lesson is not that every relationship scandal hides a conspiracy.
It is that human power is fragile, pride is dangerous, fear can enslave us, and even those who appear strongest may be desperately trying to hold together something they cannot ultimately control.
And the answer to that brokenness is not to become more like Abner.
Or to cling more tightly like Ish-bosheth.
It is to look to Jesus Christ.
The true and greater Son of David.
The King who was crowned with thorns before being revealed in resurrection glory.
The Savior who does not need to manipulate the weak to establish His reign.
The Lord who calls sinners to repentance and receives all who come to Him in faith.
The One who can take a life marked by shame and make it a testimony of grace.
Not by pretending the past never happened.
Not by removing every earthly consequence.
But by forgiving sin, giving new life, and teaching redeemed people to walk in truth.
Maybe your story contains betrayal.
Maybe it contains regret.
Maybe it contains a mistake that still makes you ashamed.
Maybe you have spent years defending an identity that is slowly falling apart.
Maybe you have been trying to keep a crown that was never meant to save you.
Today, hear the invitation of the Gospel.
Lay down your pride.
Bring your fear to Christ.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Repent of what needs to change.
Receive the mercy you could never earn.
And follow the King who gave Himself for sinners.
Because your greatest hope was never the throne you were trying to protect.
It was always the Savior who was willing to carry a cross for you.
The crown you are terrified of losing may be the very thing keeping you from seeing the King who will never let His redeemed people go.
